name: 01_basics_callback_flow.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: the three-callback flow (OnInitialize -> OnPreLayout ->
-- OnLayout) and the stateless contract behind it.
--
-- OnPreLayout confirms Base values (global/camera, and anything that
-- affects character/part count such as text or tracking) BEFORE layout is
-- generated. OnLayout then adjusts the already-generated characters/parts;
-- it can read the confirmed Base but cannot write to it.
--
-- Both callbacks are pure functions of ctx: the host may evaluate frames out
-- of order (scrubbing, caching, parallel render), so results must depend
-- only on ctx.time / ctx.frame, never on a value remembered from a previous
-- call. `ctx.global.rotation = ctx.global.rotation + 1.0` would NOT spin
-- forever -- every frame restarts from the inspector value, so this always
-- evaluates to "inspector value + 1 degree", not an accumulating spin.

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    -- Correct: closed-form function of ctx.time, safe to evaluate for any
    -- frame in any order.
    ctx.global.rotation = ctx.time * 20.0

    -- Wrong (left commented out on purpose): this looks like "advance by 1
    -- degree per frame", but ctx.global.rotation is rebuilt from the host
    -- inspector value on every call, so it never accumulates.
    -- ctx.global.rotation = ctx.global.rotation + 1.0
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- ctx.global.rotation here is the CONFIRMED value from OnPreLayout
    -- above (read-only at this point), not the raw inspector value.
    -- print("confirmed global rotation =", ctx.global.rotation)

    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        -- Also a pure function of (ctx.time, index): scrubbing backward or
        -- rendering frames out of order reproduces the exact same motion.
        character.rotation = math.sin(ctx.time * 2.0 + index * 0.2) * 15.0
    end
end
description: Reference: the three-callback flow (OnInitialize -> OnPreLayout -> OnLayout) and the stateless contract behind it.

name: 02_mt_storage.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: mt.storage (written only in OnInitialize, read-only afterward)
-- and ctx.meta.instance_seed for per-character variance without host-text or
-- count-dependent init. OnInitialize does not expose text / font_name /
-- char_count / part_count; those belong to pre_layout / layout.

function OnInitialize(ctx)
    -- Count-independent constants are fine in storage.
    mt.storage.amplitude = 0.06
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- Prefer instance_seed + mt.random*: closed-form, survives text growth, and
    -- differs across instances of the same script (a fixed literal seed would
    -- repeat the same pattern on every instance).
    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        local phase = mt.random_range(ctx.meta.instance_seed, index, 0.0, math.pi * 2.0)
        character.offset_y = 0.5 + math.sin(ctx.time * 2.0 + phase) * mt.storage.amplitude
        character.rotation = math.sin(ctx.time * 1.5 + phase) * 4.0
    end

    -- Writing to mt.storage outside OnInitialize raises a Lua error;
    -- uncomment to verify.
    -- mt.storage.amplitude = 0.0
end
description: Reference: mt.storage (written only in OnInitialize, read-only afterward) and ctx.meta.instance_seed for per-character variance without host-text or count-dependent init. OnInitialize does not expose text / font_name / char_count / part_count; those belong to pre_layout / layout.

name: 03_mt_timeline.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 3
-- Reference: ctx.timeline and mt.timeline.* -- the anchor x speed design
-- rule behind every timed animation (see scripting_api.md section 4.1).
--
-- Two axes decide how to time an animation:
--   1. Anchor  -- where is it pinned: clip start, clip end, or the whole clip?
--   2. Speed   -- real seconds (constant speed) or clip-relative progress
--                 (stretches/compresses with clip length)?
--
-- The default speed is REAL SECONDS (ctx.time). Only "whole-span" motion
-- (a drift/sweep/reveal meant to fill the entire clip) should use progress.
-- Everything else (intro, outro, typewriter, stagger) should be driven by
-- ctx.time so retiming the clip does not slow down or speed up the motion.

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    -- ctx.timeline fields, all clip-local (clip start is always frame/time 0).
    -- print("available", ctx.timeline.available)
    -- print("start_frame/end_frame", ctx.timeline.start_frame, ctx.timeline.end_frame)
    -- print("duration_seconds", ctx.timeline.duration_seconds)
    -- print("progress (0..1)", ctx.timeline.progress)

    -- available is false when the host cannot resolve a finite clip range
    -- (for example scripting in isolation); the other fields fall back to 0
    -- in that case, so always guard clip-length-dependent logic with it.

    -- Whole-span motion (drift across the ENTIRE clip): this is the one
    -- case where clip-relative progress is correct, since the drift should
    -- take longer if the clip is longer. Base values (ctx.global) can only
    -- be written here, in OnPreLayout.
    local sweepProgress = mt.timeline.progress(ctx)
    ctx.global.position_x = 0.5 + (sweepProgress - 0.5) * 0.1
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- WRONG for a fixed-speed reveal: typing speed changes with clip length.
    -- local visible = math.floor(mt.timeline.progress(ctx) * ctx.char_count)

    -- RIGHT: constant 0.12s per character regardless of clip length.
    local secondsPerCharacter = 0.12
    local visibleCount = math.floor(ctx.time / secondsPerCharacter)

    -- Intro anchored to clip start, outro anchored to clip end, both at a
    -- fixed real-time speed (auto-compressed only if the clip is shorter
    -- than introSeconds + outroSeconds). ctx.global is read-only by this
    -- point, so the fade is applied per-character instead.
    local introProgress, outroProgress = mt.timeline.intro_outro_seconds(ctx, 0.6, 0.6)
    local introOutroFade = mt.ease.out_cubic(introProgress) * (1.0 - mt.ease.in_cubic(outroProgress))

    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        character.opacity = introOutroFade
        if index > visibleCount then
            character.opacity = 0.0
        end
    end

    -- Outro fade over the last 0.4s of the clip, anchored to the clip end --
    -- built from mt.timeline.remaining directly, for cases that need only
    -- the outro half.
    local outroFade = mt.clamp(mt.timeline.remaining(ctx) / 0.4, 0.0, 1.0)
    -- ctx.chars[1].scale = 1.0 - (1.0 - outroFade) * 0.2
end
description: Reference: ctx.timeline and mt.timeline.* -- the anchor x speed design rule behind every timed animation (see scripting_api.md section 4.1).

name: 04_global.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @required 3d
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: ctx.global fields (OnPreLayout only).
-- Transform, color, gradient, stroke, and shadow are grouped in the order
-- they are applied. Each field is animated on its own cycle so its effect
-- is unambiguous during playback. Comment/uncomment a group to isolate it.

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    -- Transform: position is 0..1 canvas fraction, rotation/yaw/pitch in
    -- degrees, pivot is the point transforms are applied around.
    ctx.global.position_x = 0.5 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.1) * 0.05
    ctx.global.position_y = 0.5
    ctx.global.rotation = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.2) * 10.0
    -- ctx.global.yaw = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.1) * 15.0 -- 3D preset only
    -- ctx.global.pitch = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.13) * 10.0 -- 3D preset only
    ctx.global.scale = 1.0 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.25) * 0.1
    ctx.global.stretch_x = 1.0
    ctx.global.stretch_y = 1.0
    ctx.global.pivot_x = 0.5
    ctx.global.pivot_y = 0.5
    -- Opacity multiplies with the character and part opacity below and
    -- applies to fill, gradient, stroke, shadow, and the bounding box alike.
    ctx.global.opacity = 0.5 + mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.15)) * 0.5

    -- Fill color and optional gradient overlay; the gradient angle spins.
    ctx.global.fill.color = { r = 1.0, g = 1.0, b = 1.0, a = 1.0 }
    -- ctx.global.fill.transparent = true -- keep stroke/shadow, hide fill
    ctx.global.gradient.color_space = "oklab" -- "none" disables the gradient
    ctx.global.gradient.end_color = { r = 0.2, g = 0.6, b = 1.0, a = 1.0 }
    ctx.global.gradient.midpoint = 0.5 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.2) * 0.3
    ctx.global.gradient.angle = ctx.time * 30.0
    ctx.global.gradient.start_position = 0.0
    ctx.global.gradient.end_position = 1.0

    -- Stroke outline, pulsing width.
    ctx.global.stroke.width = 0.01 + mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.3)) * 0.02
    ctx.global.stroke.gap = 0.0
    ctx.global.stroke.color = { r = 0.0, g = 0.0, b = 0.0, a = 1.0 }
    ctx.global.stroke.order = "stroke_over_fill" -- or "fill_over_stroke"
    ctx.global.stroke.join = "round"
    ctx.global.stroke.miter_limit = 4.0

    -- Drop shadow, sweeping angle.
    ctx.global.shadow.enabled = true
    ctx.global.shadow.distance = 1.5 + mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.2)) * 2.0
    ctx.global.shadow.angle = ctx.time * 60.0
    ctx.global.shadow.color = { r = 0.0, g = 0.0, b = 0.0, a = 0.5 }
end
description: Reference: ctx.global fields (OnPreLayout only). Transform, color, gradient, stroke, and shadow are grouped in the order they are applied. Each field is animated on its own cycle so its effect is unambiguous during playback. Comment/uncomment a group to isolate it.

name: 05_camera.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @required 3d
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: ctx.camera fields (OnPreLayout only, 3D preset only).
-- Enable "3D Projection" on the inspector before playback.

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    -- Target: the point the camera looks at, in host-normalized
    -- coordinates. Y grows upward.
    ctx.camera.target_x = 0.5
    ctx.camera.target_y = 0.5

    -- Orbit angles in degrees, sweeping back and forth.
    ctx.camera.yaw = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.1) * 25.0
    ctx.camera.pitch = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.07, math.pi / 2.0) * 12.0

    -- Perspective strength: higher values exaggerate depth.
    ctx.camera.perspective = 0.55 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.08) * 0.25

    -- Zoom multiplier: higher values move the camera closer.
    ctx.camera.zoom = 1.0 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.12) * 0.1

    -- Lens shift: principal-point offset as a canvas fraction, independent
    -- of the orbit angles. Y grows upward.
    ctx.camera.lens_shift_x = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.06) * 0.03
    ctx.camera.lens_shift_y = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.09, math.pi / 2.0) * 0.02
end
description: Reference: ctx.camera fields (OnPreLayout only, 3D preset only). Enable "3D Projection" on the inspector before playback.

name: 06_character.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @required 3d
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: per-character fields, read via ctx.chars[index] (OnLayout
-- only). Only the second character (index 2) is animated so its effect
-- stands out against the untouched neighbors.

function OnLayout(ctx)
    if ctx.char_count < 2 then
        return
    end

    local character = ctx.chars[2]

    -- Read-only identity and geometry.
    -- print(character.index, character.text, character.line_index)
    -- print(character.geometry.bounds_center_x, character.geometry.bounds_center_y)

    -- Transform: offset is 0.5-centered (0.5 = no displacement), pivot is
    -- the point rotation/scale are applied around, in host-normalized
    -- coordinates. Y grows upward.
    character.offset_x = 0.5
    character.offset_y = 0.5 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.5) * 0.08
    character.pivot_x = 0.5
    character.pivot_y = 0.5
    character.scale = 1.0 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.4) * 0.3
    character.stretch_x = 1.0
    character.stretch_y = 1.0
    character.rotation = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.3) * 20.0
    -- character.z = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.2) * 0.3 -- 3D preset only
    -- character.yaw = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.2) * 20.0 -- 3D preset only
    -- character.pitch = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.25) * 10.0 -- 3D preset only
    -- Opacity multiplies with ctx.global.opacity and the owning parts' opacity.
    character.opacity = 0.4 + mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.6)) * 0.6

    -- Per-character fill overrides the global fill only while fill.use
    -- is true; hue cycles over time.
    character.fill.use = true
    character.fill.color = mt.color.from_hsv(mt.cycle(ctx.time, 3.0), 0.8, 1.0, 1.0)

    -- Per-character stroke overrides the global stroke width/gap/color
    -- only while stroke.use is true.
    -- character.stroke.use = true
    -- character.stroke.width = 0.01 + mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.3)) * 0.02
    -- character.stroke.gap = 0.0
    -- character.stroke.color = { r = 0.0, g = 0.0, b = 0.0, a = 1.0 }

    -- Per-character shadow color overrides the global shadow color only
    -- while shadow.use is true.
    -- character.shadow.use = true
    -- character.shadow.color = { r = 0.0, g = 0.0, b = 0.3, a = 0.6 }
end
description: Reference: per-character fields, read via ctx.chars[index] (OnLayout only). Only the second character (index 2) is animated so its effect stands out against the untouched neighbors.

name: 07_part.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: per-part fields, read via ctx.parts[index] (OnLayout only).
-- A "part" is a sub-piece of a character (for example a stroke component);
-- character_index / index_in_character map a part back to its owner:
--   - character_index    -- which character owns this part (1-based)
--   - index_in_character -- which of THAT character's own parts this is
--                            (1-based, restarts at 1 for every character)
--
-- Most Latin letters are a single part, which makes multi-part characters
-- hard to spot. "%=%" is forced here because "%" is made of several
-- disconnected strokes (2 circles + a slash) and "=" is 2 bars, so each
-- character's owned parts are clearly visible as separate pieces, not the
-- whole glyph.
--
-- Characters 1 and 3 are both "%" -- the SAME glyph, but two SEPARATE
-- characters, each with its own parts. This sample deliberately animates a
-- DIFFERENT index_in_character on each so the two "%" look different even
-- though they are the same glyph:
--   - character 1 ("%"): only index_in_character 1 (its first stroke)
--   - character 2 ("="): only index_in_character 1 (its top bar)
--   - character 3 ("%"): only index_in_character 2 (its SECOND stroke --
--     a different part than character 1 touches, despite the same glyph)

local function findPartByIndexInCharacter(ctx, character, targetIndexInCharacter)
    local found = nil
    for offset = 0, character.part_count - 1 do
        local part = ctx.parts[character.part_start + offset]
        if part.index_in_character == targetIndexInCharacter then
            found = part
        end
    end
    return found
end

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    ctx.global.text = "%=%"
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    if ctx.char_count < 3 then
        return
    end

    -- Character 1 ("%"): animate only index_in_character 1.
    local firstCharacter = ctx.chars[1]
    local firstPart = findPartByIndexInCharacter(ctx, firstCharacter, 1)
    if firstPart ~= nil then
        firstPart.offset_y = 0.5 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.6) * 0.06
        firstPart.scale = 1.0 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.35) * 0.2
        firstPart.fill.use = true
        firstPart.fill.color = mt.color.from_hsv(mt.cycle(ctx.time, 2.5), 0.7, 1.0, 1.0)
    end

    -- Character 2 ("="): animate its index_in_character 1 (the top bar),
    -- leaving any remaining parts of this character untouched, so the two
    -- bars of "=" visibly move independently of each other.
    local secondCharacter = ctx.chars[2]
    local secondPart = findPartByIndexInCharacter(ctx, secondCharacter, 1)
    if secondPart ~= nil then
        secondPart.rotation = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.4) * 15.0
        secondPart.stroke.use = true
        secondPart.stroke.width = 0.01 + mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.3)) * 0.1
        secondPart.stroke.color = mt.color.from_hsv(mt.cycle(ctx.time, 4.0), 0.6, 1.0, 1.0)
    end

    -- Character 3 ("%"): same glyph as character 1, but animate
    -- index_in_character 2 instead of 1 -- a DIFFERENT part of the glyph,
    -- and (because this is a separate character) never the same ctx.parts
    -- entry that character 1 touched above.
    local thirdCharacter = ctx.chars[3]
    local thirdPart = findPartByIndexInCharacter(ctx, thirdCharacter, 2)
    if thirdPart ~= nil then
        -- Read-only identity and geometry.
        -- print(thirdPart.index, thirdPart.character_index, thirdPart.index_in_character)
        -- print(thirdPart.geometry.canvas_center_x, thirdPart.geometry.canvas_center_y)
        -- print(thirdPart.geometry.local_center_x, thirdPart.geometry.local_center_y)

        -- Transform: offset is 0.5-centered (0.5 = no displacement), pivot
        -- is the point rotation/scale are applied around, in
        -- host-normalized coordinates. Y grows upward.
        thirdPart.offset_x = 0.5
        thirdPart.offset_y = 0.5 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.6) * 0.06
        thirdPart.pivot_x = 0.5
        thirdPart.pivot_y = 0.5
        thirdPart.scale = 1.0 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.35) * 0.2
        thirdPart.stretch_x = 1.0
        thirdPart.stretch_y = 1.0
        thirdPart.rotation = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.4) * 15.0
        -- thirdPart.z = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.2) * 0.3 -- 3D preset only
        -- thirdPart.yaw/pitch (below) are script-only: no host parameter
        -- group backs them (unlike character.yaw/pitch), so unlike
        -- thirdPart.z they stay available from scripts regardless of the
        -- Native preset -- only 3D projection actually renders their effect.
        -- thirdPart.yaw = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.2) * 20.0
        -- thirdPart.pitch = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.25) * 10.0
        -- Opacity multiplies with the owning character's opacity (and,
        -- through it, ctx.global.opacity).
        thirdPart.opacity = 0.3 + mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.7)) * 0.7

        -- Per-part fill overrides the character/global fill only while
        -- fill.use is true; hue cycles over time.
        thirdPart.fill.use = true
        thirdPart.fill.color = mt.color.from_hsv(mt.cycle(ctx.time, 2.5), 0.7, 1.0, 1.0)

        -- Per-part stroke/shadow overrides the character's resolved
        -- stroke/shadow only while their .use flag is true. No host
        -- parameter group backs these (cut from the inspector to keep the
        -- per-part parameter count down), so they are always available
        -- from scripts regardless of the Native preset; pulsing
        -- width/color here demonstrates that a single part can look
        -- completely different from its siblings and from the
        -- character-level stroke/shadow.
        thirdPart.stroke.use = true
        thirdPart.stroke.width = 0.01 + mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.3)) * 0.1
        thirdPart.stroke.gap = 0.0
        thirdPart.stroke.color = mt.color.from_hsv(mt.cycle(ctx.time, 4.0), 0.6, 1.0, 1.0)
        thirdPart.shadow.use = true
        thirdPart.shadow.color = { r = 0.0, g = 0.0, b = 0.3, a = 0.6 }
    end
end
description: Reference: per-part fields, read via ctx.parts[index] (OnLayout only). A "part" is a sub-piece of a character (for example a stroke component); character_index / index_in_character map a part back to its owner:   - character_index    -- which character owns this part (1-based)   - index_in_character -- which of THAT character's own parts this is                            (1-based, restarts at 1 for every character)

name: 08_inheritance.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 6
-- Reference: the inheritance chain (scripting_api.md section 8).
--
--   Global (confirmed in OnPreLayout)
--     -> character: use=true picks the raw per-character value, use=false
--        falls through to Global
--     -> part: use=true picks the raw per-part value, use=false falls
--        through to the owning character's resolved value
--
-- fill/stroke/shadow all follow this exact chain. A gradient only paints
-- the parts of the chain that fell all the way through to Global (both the
-- character's AND the part's fill.use are false); anywhere fill.use is true
-- is painted as a flat color instead, regardless of the gradient.
--
-- Each character/part below flips its OWN fill.use on and off over time, so
-- the exact moment a flat individual color takes over from (or falls back
-- to) the inherited gradient is visible during playback, not just a static
-- comparison.
--
-- Text should have at least 3 characters; character 3 needs at least 1 part.

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    -- Global fill is white, but the gradient overlay repaints anything that
    -- is not using an individual color.
    ctx.global.fill.color = { r = 1.0, g = 1.0, b = 1.0, a = 1.0 }
    ctx.global.gradient.color_space = "oklab"
    ctx.global.gradient.end_color = { r = 0.2, g = 0.6, b = 1.0, a = 1.0 }
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- Character 1: fill.use toggles on a slow square wave. While it is
    -- false, this character is painted by the gradient like the rest of
    -- the untouched text; the instant it flips to true, a flat red wins
    -- over the gradient entirely.
    if ctx.char_count >= 1 then
        local character = ctx.chars[1]
        character.fill.use = mt.wave_square(ctx.time, 0.2) > 0.0
        character.fill.color = { r = 1.0, g = 0.2, b = 0.2, a = 1.0 }
    end

    -- Character 2: fill.use stays true throughout, but the flat color
    -- itself cycles hue -- contrast this with character 1's on/off flip.
    if ctx.char_count >= 2 then
        local character = ctx.chars[2]
        character.fill.use = true
        character.fill.color = mt.color.from_hsv(mt.cycle(ctx.time, 3.0), 0.8, 1.0)
    end

    -- Character 3, part 1: the character's OWN fill.use stays false
    -- (inherits Global/gradient throughout), but the first owned part
    -- toggles fill.use on its own square wave -- out of phase with
    -- character 1 -- so only that one part ever differs from its
    -- character, and only while its own toggle is on.
    if ctx.char_count >= 3 and ctx.part_count >= 1 then
        local character = ctx.chars[3]
        if character.part_count >= 1 then
            local part = ctx.parts[character.part_start]
            part.fill.use = mt.wave_square(ctx.time, 0.2, math.pi) > 0.0
            part.fill.color = { r = 0.2, g = 1.0, b = 0.4, a = 1.0 }
        end
    end

    -- Shadow color follows the exact same chain as fill: a character's
    -- resolved shadow.color propagates down to its owned parts unless a
    -- part sets shadow.use = true itself.
    -- ctx.chars[1].shadow.use = true
    -- ctx.chars[1].shadow.color = { r = 0.0, g = 0.0, b = 0.0, a = 0.6 }
end
description: Reference: the inheritance chain (scripting_api.md section 8).

name: 09_bounding_box.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: ctx.bounding_box fields (OnLayout only) -- the box/frame drawn
-- around the transformed text. See 10_output.lua for ctx.output (write-on
-- reveal and draw order), a separate, independent feature.

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- The box outline itself, all 4 edges drawn with rounded caps.
    ctx.bounding_box.enabled = true
    ctx.bounding_box.draw_top = true
    ctx.bounding_box.draw_bottom = true
    ctx.bounding_box.draw_left = true
    ctx.bounding_box.draw_right = true
    ctx.bounding_box.color = { r = 1.0, g = 1.0, b = 1.0, a = 1.0 }
    ctx.bounding_box.start_cap = "round" -- see MtBoundingBox for valid caps
    ctx.bounding_box.end_cap = "round"
    ctx.bounding_box.corner_radius = 1.0

    -- Outline width pulses so the stroke's own animation is unambiguous.
    ctx.bounding_box.width = 3.0 + mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.25)) * 6.0

    -- Margin between the text and the box breathes in and out, so the box
    -- itself visibly grows/shrinks around the (otherwise static) text.
    local margin = 2.0 + mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.2)) * 8.0
    ctx.bounding_box.margin_x = margin
    ctx.bounding_box.margin_y = margin

    -- Fill behind the text, independent of the outline; opacity cycles.
    ctx.bounding_box.fill_enabled = true
    ctx.bounding_box.fill_color = { r = 0.0, g = 0.0, b = 0.0, a = 1.0 }
    ctx.bounding_box.fill_opacity = 0.15 + mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.3)) * 0.3

    -- Fill and stroke can be nudged independently of each other and of the
    -- text/margin above (for a detached-shadow-like offset look).
    ctx.bounding_box.fill_offset_x = 0.0
    ctx.bounding_box.fill_offset_y = 0.0
    ctx.bounding_box.stroke_offset_x = 0.0
    ctx.bounding_box.stroke_offset_y = 0.0
end
description: Reference: ctx.bounding_box fields (OnLayout only) -- the box/frame drawn around the transformed text. See 10_output.lua for ctx.output (write-on reveal and draw order), a separate, independent feature.

name: 10_output.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: ctx.output fields (OnLayout only) -- write-on reveal range and
-- draw order, independent of ctx.bounding_box (see 09_bounding_box.lua).

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- Write-on reveal range, normalized 0.0..1.0 across the whole sequence.
    -- write_on_mode selects whether that range advances through characters
    -- or parts. Here the reveal sweeps forward and back on a 4-second
    -- cycle, so characters visibly appear and disappear in text order.
    ctx.output.write_on_mode = "character" -- or "part"
    ctx.output.write_on_start = 0.0
    ctx.output.write_on_end = mt.pingpong(ctx.time, 4.0)

    -- Manual reveal and draw order overrides the natural text order; see
    -- MtOutput for the manual_order_text syntax. Uncomment to reveal
    -- characters 3, then 1, then 2 instead of left-to-right.
    -- ctx.output.manual_order_enabled = true
    -- ctx.output.manual_order_text = "3,1,2"

    -- reorder_parts affects only multi-part characters (for example CJK
    -- strokes or symbols like "%"/"="), so it has no visible effect on
    -- plain single-part Latin text.
    -- ctx.output.reorder_parts = true
end
description: Reference: ctx.output fields (OnLayout only) -- write-on reveal range and draw order, independent of ctx.bounding_box (see 09_bounding_box.lua).

name: 11_layout_shaping.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 12
-- Reference: ctx.global text-shaping fields (OnPreLayout only).
-- Each field is animated on its own cycle so its effect is unambiguous
-- when scrubbing or during playback. Comment/uncomment fields to isolate
-- one at a time.
--
-- Text is forced to 3 lines here (a "\n"-separated string) because
-- line_spacing has no visible effect on single-line text.

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    -- Text and font can be reassigned; font_name must be one of ctx.fonts.
    ctx.global.text = "Line one\nLine two\nLine three"
    -- ctx.global.font_name = ctx.fonts[1]

    -- Extra spacing added between characters, breathing in and out.
    ctx.global.tracking = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.2) * 0.06

    -- Multiplies the distance between lines.
    ctx.global.line_spacing = 1.0 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.15) * 0.4

    -- Switches to vertical (top-to-bottom) writing.
    -- ctx.global.vertical = true

    -- Horizontal alignment: "left" | "center" | "right". Cycled on a
    -- 3-second step so each value is visibly held, not blended.
    local horizontalAlignments = { "left", "center", "right" }
    local horizontalStep = math.floor(mt.cycle(ctx.time, 3.0) * #horizontalAlignments) + 1
    ctx.global.h_align = horizontalAlignments[horizontalStep]

    -- Vertical alignment: "top" | "center" | "bottom" | "baseline". Cycled
    -- independently on its own 4-second step.
    local verticalAlignments = { "top", "center", "bottom", "baseline" }
    local verticalStep = math.floor(mt.cycle(ctx.time, 4.0) * #verticalAlignments) + 1
    ctx.global.v_align = verticalAlignments[verticalStep]

    -- Per-character extra margin, indexed from 1. Missing indices default
    -- to zero, so a short table only affects the first characters. Here
    -- the margin before the second character pulses over time.
    ctx.global.margins = { 0.0, mt.saturate(mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.3)) * 0.12 }
end
description: Reference: ctx.global text-shaping fields (OnPreLayout only). Each field is animated on its own cycle so its effect is unambiguous when scrubbing or during playback. Comment/uncomment fields to isolate one at a time.

name: 12_mt_color.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: mt.color.* construction and interpolation helpers.
-- All return a new color table; none mutate their arguments.

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- from_hsv builds an RGBA color from normalized hue/saturation/value.
    local hueColor = mt.color.from_hsv(0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.0)

    -- from_oklch builds an RGBA color from the perceptually-uniform OKLCH
    -- space (lightness, chroma, hue); useful when interpolating hues needs
    -- to look perceptually even, unlike raw HSV interpolation.
    local oklchColor = mt.color.from_oklch(0.75, 0.15, 0.6, 1.0)

    -- lerp interpolates two RGBA color tables component-wise.
    local red = { r = 1.0, g = 0.0, b = 0.0, a = 1.0 }
    local blue = { r = 0.0, g = 0.0, b = 1.0, a = 1.0 }
    local mixed = mt.color.lerp(red, blue, 0.5)

    -- with_alpha copies a color while replacing only its alpha channel.
    local translucentRed = mt.color.with_alpha(red, 0.4)

    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        local hue = mt.distribute(index, ctx.char_count)
        character.fill.use = true
        character.fill.color = mt.color.from_hsv(hue, 0.75, 1.0, 1.0)
    end

    -- Uncomment to inspect the constructed colors directly.
    -- print(hueColor.r, hueColor.g, hueColor.b, hueColor.a)
    -- print(oklchColor.r, oklchColor.g, oklchColor.b)
    -- print(mixed.r, mixed.g, mixed.b)
    -- print(translucentRed.a)
end

name: 13_mt_math.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: mt.* range/interpolation helpers that take fixed inputs
-- (not time), so they are printed to the Debug Console rather than
-- animated. See 14_mt_stagger.lua, 15_mt_random_noise.lua, and
-- 16_mt_physics_waves.lua for the time-driven counterparts.
--
-- IMPORTANT: this sample is print-driven, not visual. Watch VSCode's OUTPUT
-- panel, channel "MT Sim" (View > Output, then pick "MT Sim" from the
-- dropdown), while playing/scrubbing -- the on-screen rainbow coloring in
-- OnLayout only demonstrates mt.distribute, not the other functions listed
-- below.

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    print("clamp(1.5, 0, 1) =", mt.clamp(1.5, 0.0, 1.0))
    print("saturate(1.5) =", mt.saturate(1.5))
    print("lerp(0, 10, 0.3) =", mt.lerp(0.0, 10.0, 0.3))
    print("inverse_lerp(0, 10, 3) =", mt.inverse_lerp(0.0, 10.0, 3.0))

    -- remap maps a value from one range to another; clamped=true clamps the
    -- normalized position into 0..1 before mapping, so out-of-range inputs
    -- saturate instead of extrapolating.
    print("remap(3, 0, 10, 0, 100) =", mt.remap(3.0, 0.0, 10.0, 0.0, 100.0, true))
    print("remap(15, 0, 10, 0, 100, clamped) =", mt.remap(15.0, 0.0, 10.0, 0.0, 100.0, true))

    -- wrap folds a value into the half-open range [low, high); useful for
    -- normalizing angles or hues that cycle past their range.
    print("wrap(370, 0, 360) =", mt.wrap(370.0, 0.0, 360.0))

    -- lerp_angle interpolates degrees along the SHORTEST path, avoiding the
    -- long way around that a plain lerp would take across the 0/360 seam.
    print("lerp_angle(350, 10, 0.5) =", mt.lerp_angle(350.0, 10.0, 0.5))

    -- smoothstep: 0..1 Hermite transition between two edges, flat-velocity
    -- at both ends -- a common way to add ease to a linear progress value.
    print("smoothstep(0, 1, 0.5) =", mt.smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, 0.5))
    print("smoothstep(0, 1, 0.25) =", mt.smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, 0.25))

    -- distribute maps a one-based index evenly across 0..1; useful for
    -- assigning each character a stable position-derived value (hue,
    -- delay, ...).
    print("distribute(1, 5) =", mt.distribute(1, 5))
    print("distribute(5, 5) =", mt.distribute(5, 5))
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- distribute driving a per-character value: first character at 0.0,
    -- last character at 1.0, evenly spaced in between.
    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        local position = mt.distribute(index, ctx.char_count)
        character.fill.use = true
        character.fill.color = mt.color.from_hsv(position, 0.7, 1.0)
    end
end
description: Reference: mt.* range/interpolation helpers that take fixed inputs (not time), so they are printed to the Debug Console rather than animated. See 14_mt_stagger.lua, 15_mt_random_noise.lua, and 16_mt_physics_waves.lua for the time-driven counterparts.

name: 14_mt_stagger.lua

-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 3
-- Reference: mt.stagger and mt.stagger_pattern -- the standard building
-- block for "characters animate one after another" effects.
--
-- mt.stagger(time, index, delay, duration): index i starts delay*(i-1)
-- seconds after index 1, then ramps 0..1 over duration seconds. The
-- animation itself (what to DO with that 0..1 progress) is entirely up to
-- the caller -- here it drives an ease-out rise.
--
-- Looped on a repeating window so the whole cascade replays continuously.

local kDelay = 0.08
local kDuration = 0.4
local kLoopPeriod = 2.0

function OnLayout(ctx)
    local loopedTime = ctx.time % kLoopPeriod

    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]

        character.offset_y = 0.5 + (1.0 - mt.ease.out_cubic(progress)) * 0.15
    end

    -- mt.stagger_pattern adds a 'pattern' argument that controls which
    -- index starts first: 'asc' (left-to-right, same as mt.stagger),
    -- 'desc' (right-to-left, alias 'right_to_left'), 'center' (center
    -- outward), or 'random' (shuffled by seed). Uncomment one line at a

name: 15_mt_random_noise.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: mt.random / mt.random_range / mt.noise1 / mt.noise2 --
-- deterministic randomness safe to call every frame, directly inside
-- OnLayout, without storing anything in mt.storage.
--
-- Unlike math.random (which depends on call order and is unsafe for
-- per-character variance in a stateless callback), mt.random(seed, index)
-- always returns the same value for the same (seed, index) pair, so
-- scrubbing or rendering frames out of order reproduces identical results.

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    -- Same (seed, index) always returns the same [0, 1) value.
    print("random(seed=1, index=3) =", mt.random(1, 3))
    print("random(seed=1, index=3) again =", mt.random(1, 3))

    -- Different index in the same seed's series gives a different value.
    print("random(seed=1, index=4) =", mt.random(1, 4))

    -- random_range remaps the [0, 1) result into [low, high).
    print("random_range(seed=1, index=3, 10, 20) =", mt.random_range(1, 3, 10.0, 20.0))

    -- A little extra tracking gives independently-rotating characters more
    -- room before their corners can reach a neighbor (see the OnLayout
    -- comments below), without changing how any of the mt.* calls work.
    ctx.global.tracking = 0.03
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- Stable per-character jitter: each character gets its own fixed
    -- random offset, unrelated to its neighbors, with no mt.storage needed.
    -- offset_x is a DISPLACEMENT from the character's own natural position
    -- (0.5 = no displacement), so the jitter is added to the current value,
    -- not assigned in place of it -- assigning 0.5 + jitter directly would
    -- collapse every character onto the same spot near canvas center,
    -- overlapping them instead of nudging each one from where it already is.
    --
    -- offset_x is normalized to CANVAS WIDTH, not to the character's own
    -- size (see section 7.2's warning): a fixed guess like +-0.02 can be
    -- many times the character's own advance width and overlap neighbors.
    -- Scale the jitter to a fraction of this character's own advance_x
    -- (its normalized advance width, tracking/margins excluded) instead of
    -- guessing an absolute canvas-relative number.
    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        local jitterFraction = mt.random_range(100, index, -0.02, 0.02)
        character.offset_x = character.offset_x + character.geometry.advance_x * jitterFraction
    end

    -- noise1: smooth (not jittery) 1D value noise, continuous between
    -- integer sample points. Feeding time into the SAMPLE POSITION (first
    -- argument) produces organic wobble over time; offsetting that same
    -- position by index gives each character an independent phase. The
    -- seed (second argument) only selects a different noise pattern
    -- overall -- passing index there does NOT reliably separate
    -- neighboring characters, since noise1 is continuous and nearby
    -- sample positions correlate regardless of seed.
    --
    -- The sample position must advance through several integer lattice
    -- points over the sample's @duration for the wobble to read clearly;
    -- too slow a rate (for example ctx.time * 0.8, crossing under 1 lattice
    -- point in 5 seconds) can land on a stretch where noise1 happens to be
    -- nearly flat, making the motion look broken when it is just slow.
    --
    -- Amplitude is capped at +-4.0 degrees, safe here because
    -- OnPreLayout added a bit of extra tracking above: with character
    -- spacing at only the font's own default advance width, rotating
    -- independently past roughly +-2 degrees would make the corners of
    -- neighboring characters visibly overlap even with zero positional
    -- jitter -- a geometry limit of the layout, not a defect in noise1.
    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        character.rotation = mt.noise1(ctx.time * 2.5 + index) * 4.0
    end

    -- noise2: same idea in 2D -- one axis time, one axis position, for
    -- motion that appears to flow spatially across the characters. As
    -- with noise1 above, the time axis must move through several lattice
    -- points during @duration for the wobble to be visible.
    if ctx.char_count >= 1 then
        local position = mt.distribute(1, math.max(ctx.char_count, 1))
        ctx.chars[1].offset_y = 0.5 + mt.noise2(ctx.time * 2.5, position * 4.0) * 0.05
    end
end
description: Reference: mt.random / mt.random_range / mt.noise1 / mt.noise2 -- deterministic randomness safe to call every frame, directly inside OnLayout, without storing anything in mt.storage.

name: 16_mt_physics_waves.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 8
-- Reference: mt.spring and the mt.wave family -- closed-form oscillation
-- helpers, none of which need frame-to-frame state.
--
-- Each function drives one character's vertical offset so their shapes are
-- visible side by side during playback.
--
-- Text is forced to 12 non-space characters here, arranged as 6 adjacent
-- PAIRS -- AB | AC | AD | AE | AF | AG -- where the first character of
-- every pair is literally the same glyph, "A", always driven by plain wave
-- (the reference sine shape), so the reference is visually identical
-- everywhere it appears. The second character of each pair is the shape
-- being compared against it, so every comparison sits in 2 side-by-side
-- characters instead of being spread across the whole row.
--
-- Amplitude is large (0.3) and frequency slow (0.5 Hz, a 2-second period)
-- so the shape differences are unmistakable frame-to-frame, not just in a
-- fast-moving screenshot.

-- Extra spacing after the 2nd character of each pair to visually separate
-- the 6 pairs: AB | AC | AD | AE | AF | AG. margins is a contiguous
-- 1-based array (no gaps), so every index up to the last boundary must be
-- filled in, using 0.0 for characters that get no extra spacing. margins
-- units are the same as tracking (1.0 ~= 1 em, i.e. roughly one full
-- character width) -- 0.7 adds a gap about 70% of a character's own
-- width, clearly wider than the normal gap between the 2 characters
-- within a pair.
local kPairBoundaryMargin = 0.7
local kCharacterCount = 12
local kPairCount = 6

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    ctx.global.text = "ABACADAEAFAG"

    local margins = {}
    for index = 1, kCharacterCount do
        margins[index] = 0.0
    end
    margins[2] = kPairBoundaryMargin -- after "B", before the next pair's "A"
    margins[4] = kPairBoundaryMargin -- after "C", before the next pair's "A"
    margins[6] = kPairBoundaryMargin -- after "D", before the next pair's "A"
    margins[8] = kPairBoundaryMargin -- after "E", before the next pair's "A"
    margins[10] = kPairBoundaryMargin -- after "F", before the next pair's "A"
    ctx.global.margins = margins
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- Color each pair of characters distinctly (both characters in a pair
    -- share the same hue) so the AB | AC | AD | AE | AF | AG grouping
    -- reads at a glance, on top of the extra spacing from margins above.
    for _, index in ipairs({ 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 }) do
        if ctx.char_count >= index then
            local pairIndex = math.floor((index - 1) / 2)
            -- mt.distribute pins its first AND last index to the same hue
            -- (0.0 and 1.0 are the same color on the wheel), which would
            -- make the last pair look identical to the first. Divide the
            -- hue wheel into kPairCount equal steps directly instead, so
            -- all 6 pairs get distinct, evenly-spaced colors.
            local hue = pairIndex / kPairCount
            local color = mt.color.from_hsv(hue, 0.75, 1.0)
            ctx.chars[index].fill.use = true
            ctx.chars[index].fill.color = color
            if ctx.char_count >= index + 1 then
                ctx.chars[index + 1].fill.use = true
                ctx.chars[index + 1].fill.color = color
            end
        end
    end

    -- Every "A" (characters 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) is literally the same
    -- glyph, always driven by the same reference wave: sine wave
    -- shorthand, oscillates -1 to 1, easing in and out of each extreme --
    -- slows down near the top/bottom, speeds up crossing the middle.
    -- Compare each one against the character immediately after it (same
    -- frequency and amplitude in every pair).
    for _, index in ipairs({ 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 }) do
        if ctx.char_count >= index then
            ctx.chars[index].offset_y = 0.5 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.5) * 0.3
        end
    end

    -- pair 1, "AB": wave_square (character 2, "B") -- hard on/off, only
    -- ever -1 or 1. Compare against "A" right next to it: "B" is always
    -- pinned to one of exactly 2 positions and never in between, while "A"
    -- passes through every intermediate position on its way.
    if ctx.char_count >= 2 then
        ctx.chars[2].offset_y = 0.5 + mt.wave_square(ctx.time, 0.5) * 0.3
    end

    -- pair 2, "AC": wave with a phase offset (character 4, "C") -- same
    -- shape and frequency as the reference "A", just shifted in time so it
    -- does not move in lockstep with it -- compare against "A" to see a
    -- phase difference rather than a shape difference.
    if ctx.char_count >= 4 then
        ctx.chars[4].offset_y = 0.5 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.5, math.pi / 2.0) * 0.3
    end

    -- pair 3, "AD": wave_triangle (character 6, "D") -- linear ramp
    -- up/down between -1 and 1, constant speed the whole way, no easing
    -- near the top/bottom. Compare against "A" right next to it, which
    -- visibly slows down at the extremes.
    if ctx.char_count >= 6 then
        ctx.chars[6].offset_y = 0.5 + mt.wave_triangle(ctx.time, 0.5) * 0.3
    end

    -- pair 4, "AE": wave_sawtooth (character 8, "E") -- linear ramp up
    -- from -1 to just under 1, then snaps back and repeats. Compare
    -- against "A" right next to it: "E" ramps up steadily then snaps,
    -- while "A" eases up and down symmetrically with no snap.
    if ctx.char_count >= 8 then
        ctx.chars[8].offset_y = 0.5 + mt.wave_sawtooth(ctx.time, 0.5) * 0.3
    end

    -- pair 5, "AF": spring (character 10, "F") -- damped oscillation
    -- settling from 1 to 0, an "overshoot and settle" motion with no
    -- simulation loop. Retriggered here by wrapping time into a repeating
    -- sawtooth so it replays continuously. Compare against "A" right next
    -- to it (still plain wave): "F" overshoots past its resting point and
    -- settles, while "A" oscillates continuously.
    if ctx.char_count >= 10 then
        local retrigger = mt.cycle(ctx.time, 2.0) * 2.0
        ctx.chars[10].offset_y = 0.5 + mt.spring(retrigger, 4.0, 0.3) * 0.3
    end

    -- pair 6, "AG": wiggle (character 12, "G") -- layered noise-driven
    -- jitter, tunable via octaves for a more textured (less purely
    -- sinusoidal) shake than a single mt.wave. Compare against "A" right
    -- next to it: "G" wanders irregularly with no fixed period, while "A"
    -- repeats the exact same cycle every 2 seconds.
    if ctx.char_count >= 12 then
        ctx.chars[12].offset_y = 0.5 + mt.wiggle(ctx.time, 1.0, 0.3, 2, 7)
    end
end
description: Reference: mt.spring and the mt.wave family -- closed-form oscillation helpers, none of which need frame-to-frame state.

name: 17_mt_ease.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: mt.ease.* easing functions.
-- Assigns one easing function per character so the shapes of all curves
-- are visible side by side: feed the same 0..1 progress into each and use
-- the result to drive character offset_y.
--
-- Text is forced to 19 non-space characters here, one per entry in
-- functionNames below (extra characters would otherwise be ignored, and
-- the default sample text is too short to show every curve).

local functionNames = {
    "linear",
    "in_quad", "out_quad", "in_out_quad",
    "in_cubic", "out_cubic", "in_out_cubic",
    "in_sine", "out_sine", "in_out_sine",
    "in_back", "out_back", "in_out_back",
    "in_elastic", "out_elastic", "in_out_elastic",
    "in_bounce", "out_bounce", "in_out_bounce",
}

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    ctx.global.text = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRS"
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    local progress = mt.pingpong(ctx.time, 2.0)

    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        local functionName = functionNames[index]
        if functionName ~= nil then
            local eased = mt.ease[functionName](progress)
            character.offset_y = 0.5 + eased * 0.15
        end
    end

    -- cubic_bezier takes explicit control points instead of a name.
    -- local eased = mt.ease.cubic_bezier(0.42, 0.0, 0.58, 1.0, progress)
end
description: Reference: mt.ease.* easing functions. Assigns one easing function per character so the shapes of all curves are visible side by side: feed the same 0..1 progress into each and use the result to drive character offset_y.

name: 18_mt_keyframes.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 4
-- Reference: mt.keyframes -- closed-form, stateless multi-segment
-- keyframe evaluation. Useful whenever an animation has more than one
-- distinct phase (fall -> bounce -> settle -> exit) and hand-rolling it
-- with clamp + inverse_lerp would be tedious.
--
-- Each key is { t = <time>, v = <value>, ease = <optional> }; `t` must be
-- ascending. `ease` (optional, default linear) applies to the segment
-- LEADING INTO that key, and can be a named mt.ease function name (string)
-- or a custom function(t) ... end. Before the first key or after the last
-- key, the value clamps to that endpoint.

function OnLayout(ctx)
    if ctx.char_count < 1 then
        return
    end

    -- Numeric keyframes: fall in with a bounce, hold, then ease out.
    -- Looped over a repeating window so the whole sequence replays.
    local loopedTime = ctx.time % 2.0
    local keyframedOffset = mt.keyframes({
        { t = 0.0, v = -0.15 },
        { t = 0.3, v = 0.0, ease = "out_bounce" },
        { t = 1.2, v = 0.0 },
        { t = 1.6, v = -0.15, ease = "in_cubic" },
    }, loopedTime)
    ctx.chars[1].offset_y = 0.5 + keyframedOffset

    -- Color keyframes: the same function interpolates { r, g, b, a } tables
    -- directly -- no separate color-specific keyframe helper needed. A
    -- single `keys` array must be all-number or all-color, never mixed.
    if ctx.char_count >= 2 then
        local tint = mt.keyframes({
            { t = 0.0, v = { r = 1.0, g = 1.0, b = 1.0, a = 1.0 } },
            { t = 1.0, v = { r = 1.0, g = 0.4, b = 0.1, a = 1.0 }, ease = "out_cubic" },
            { t = 2.0, v = { r = 1.0, g = 1.0, b = 1.0, a = 1.0 }, ease = "in_cubic" },
        }, loopedTime)
        ctx.chars[2].fill.use = true
        ctx.chars[2].fill.color = tint
    end
end

name: 19_mt_layout_reflow.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 4
-- Reference: mt.layout.reflow -- fixes the baseline drift and broken
-- advance that a per-character scale animation causes on its own (see the
-- theory in scripting_api.md appendix A). Call it AFTER all per-character
-- scale/stretch writes for the frame, as a final re-typesetting pass.
--
-- This sample reflows the WHOLE line. See 20_mt_partial_reflow.lua
-- for re-typesetting only a sub-range of characters, anchored on one of
-- them.

local kAnchorIndex = 1

function OnLayout(ctx)
    if ctx.char_count < kAnchorIndex then
        return
    end

    -- reflow preserves the anchor's current transformed typesetting origin.
    -- Put its scale pivot on the horizontal baseline so the anchor itself
    -- cannot move the whole line vertically while its scale changes.
    local anchor = ctx.chars[kAnchorIndex]
    anchor.pivot_y = 0.5
        + anchor.geometry.canvas_origin_y
        - anchor.geometry.bounds_center_y

    -- Pass 1: any per-character size animation. Left alone, scaling around
    -- each character's own natural center would drift the baseline and
    -- crowd/gap the neighbors.
    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        character.scale = 0.6 + 0.4 * mt.stagger(ctx.time % 2.0, index, 0.1, 0.5)
    end

    -- Pass 2: re-typeset the whole line using scaled font advances and a
    -- small extra gap (as a fraction of canvas width). This does not
    -- equalize the visible ink gap between unlike glyph shapes.
    mt.layout.reflow(ctx, 0.01, { anchor = kAnchorIndex })
end

name: 20_mt_partial_reflow.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: mt.layout.reflow with `targets` and `anchor` -- reflow
-- only a SUB-RANGE of characters, anchored on one of them whose position
-- stays fixed while its neighbors re-flow around it. Characters outside
-- `targets` are left completely untouched.
--
-- Text is forced to 8 non-space characters here so the untouched
-- characters before/after the re-typeset range are clearly visible on
-- both sides.
--
-- IMPORTANT: retypeset does not persist anything between frames. If a
-- frame does not call retypeset, the target characters' offset_x/offset_y
-- fall back to their default (evenly-spaced) positions -- a previous
-- frame's alignment is NOT remembered. Any step below that needs to KEEP a
-- previously-computed layout (not just the default one) must call
-- retypeset again every single frame, even while nothing else in that step
-- is animating.
--
-- This sample cycles through the following steps, split into named
-- functions below:
--   0.0-0.5s  stepHoldFull     : target range ("CDEF") at full size,
--                                default evenly-spaced positions.
--   0.5-1.5s  stepShrink       : target range shrinks to 0.55x without
--                                calling retypeset, so each character
--                                shrinks around its own center and a gap
--                                opens between neighbors.
--   1.5-2.0s  stepHoldShrunk   : holds the shrunk size with the gap open.
--   2.0-2.5s  stepAlignShrunk  : calls retypeset at the shrunk size, which
--                                closes the gap.
--   2.5-3.5s  stepGrowOverlap  : the size on screen grows back toward full
--                                size, but retypeset keeps being called
--                                at the SHRUNK size from stepAlignShrunk,
--                                so positions stay where that packed
--                                layout put them. Since neighbors were
--                                already touching with no slack, growing
--                                the displayed size makes them overlap.
--   3.5-4.0s  stepHoldOverlap  : holds that overlapping state.
--   4.0-4.5s  stepAlignFull    : calls retypeset at the full size, which
--                                resolves the overlap.
--   4.5-5.0s  stepHoldFinal    : holds the resolved, evenly-spaced layout.
--
-- NOTE on the `gap` argument (2nd argument to retypeset, here 0): retypeset
-- only ever repositions characters INSIDE `targets` -- it has no knowledge
-- of what comes after them, so it can never reserve extra room for an
-- untouched neighbor, or for the targets themselves to grow further later.
-- A positive `gap` shrinks the slack available before the next overlap, so
-- keep it small (or 0, as here) whenever a target range sits right next to
-- an untouched character and its size may grow further afterward.

local kTargetIndices = { 3, 4, 5, 6 }
local kAnchorIndex = 3

local kShrunkScale = 0.55
local kFullScale = 1.0

local kHoldFullEnd = 0.5
local kShrinkEnd = 1.5
local kHoldShrunkEnd = 2.0
local kAlignShrunkEnd = 2.5
local kGrowOverlapEnd = 3.5
local kHoldOverlapEnd = 4.0
local kAlignFullEnd = 4.5
-- stepHoldFinal covers everything from kAlignFullEnd to the end of the clip.

-- Applies `scale` to every target character. Every step calls this itself
-- (rather than relying on a previous step's write) so each frame is fully
-- self-contained.
local function applyDisplayScale(ctx, scale)
    for _, index in ipairs(kTargetIndices) do
        if ctx.char_count >= index then
            ctx.chars[index].scale = scale
        end
    end
end

-- Runs retypeset with the target range temporarily set to `retypesetScale`
-- (which may differ from the scale that ends up displayed), then restores
-- `displayScale` for rendering. This is how a step can position characters
-- "as if" they were still at an earlier scale while showing them at a
-- different, current scale.
local function alignAtScale(ctx, retypesetScale, displayScale)
    applyDisplayScale(ctx, retypesetScale)
    mt.layout.reflow(ctx, 0.0, {
        targets = kTargetIndices,
        anchor = kAnchorIndex,
    })
    applyDisplayScale(ctx, displayScale)
end

local function stepHoldFull(ctx)
    applyDisplayScale(ctx, kFullScale)
end

local function stepShrink(ctx)
    local progress = mt.smoothstep(kHoldFullEnd, kShrinkEnd, ctx.time)
    applyDisplayScale(ctx, mt.lerp(kFullScale, kShrunkScale, progress))
end

local function stepHoldShrunk(ctx)
    applyDisplayScale(ctx, kShrunkScale)
end

local function stepAlignShrunk(ctx)
    alignAtScale(ctx, kShrunkScale, kShrunkScale)
end

local function stepGrowOverlap(ctx)
    local progress = mt.smoothstep(kAlignShrunkEnd, kGrowOverlapEnd, ctx.time)
    local displayScale = mt.lerp(kShrunkScale, kFullScale, progress)
    alignAtScale(ctx, kShrunkScale, displayScale)
end

local function stepHoldOverlap(ctx)
    alignAtScale(ctx, kShrunkScale, kFullScale)
end

local function stepAlignFull(ctx)
    alignAtScale(ctx, kFullScale, kFullScale)
end

local function stepHoldFinal(ctx)
    alignAtScale(ctx, kFullScale, kFullScale)
end

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    ctx.global.text = "ABCDEFGH"
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- Color the range being re-typeset (characters 3-6) differently from
    -- the untouched characters around it (1-2 and 7-8), so the boundary of
    -- the affected range is unmistakable.
    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        local isTarget = index >= kAnchorIndex and index <= kTargetIndices[#kTargetIndices]
        character.fill.use = true
        if isTarget then
            character.fill.color = { r = 1.0, g = 0.35, b = 0.35, a = 1.0 }
        else
            character.fill.color = { r = 0.6, g = 0.6, b = 0.6, a = 1.0 }
        end
    end

    -- Dispatch to exactly one step function based on ctx.time. Every
    -- branch, including the "nothing is animating" hold steps, fully
    -- determines this frame's scale (and, where relevant, re-runs
    -- retypeset) from ctx.time alone -- never from what a previous frame
    -- computed.
    if ctx.time < kHoldFullEnd then
        stepHoldFull(ctx)
    elseif ctx.time < kShrinkEnd then
        stepShrink(ctx)
    elseif ctx.time < kHoldShrunkEnd then
        stepHoldShrunk(ctx)
    elseif ctx.time < kAlignShrunkEnd then
        stepAlignShrunk(ctx)
    elseif ctx.time < kGrowOverlapEnd then
        stepGrowOverlap(ctx)
    elseif ctx.time < kHoldOverlapEnd then
        stepHoldOverlap(ctx)
    elseif ctx.time < kAlignFullEnd then
        stepAlignFull(ctx)
    else
        stepHoldFinal(ctx)
    end
end
description: Reference: mt.layout.reflow with `targets` and `anchor` -- reflow only a SUB-RANGE of characters, anchored on one of them whose position stays fixed while its neighbors re-flow around it. Characters outside `targets` are left completely untouched.

name: 21_mt_path.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 4
-- Reference: mt.path.* closed-form motion path helpers.
-- Character 1 arcs onto its natural position along a cubic Bezier curve.
-- Character 2 travels through 3 fixed waypoints along a Catmull-Rom spline
-- that passes exactly through each of them.
-- A part owned by character 3 travels along a fixed square drawn directly
-- in canvas coordinates, using mt.layout.place_2d, while ctx.global
-- itself is being moved/rotated/scaled/pivot-shifted.
--
-- Text should have at least 3 characters; extra characters are untouched.

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    -- Animate every ctx.global transform field at once, to demonstrate that
    -- the part below still lands at its intended canvas position no matter
    -- how the whole text is currently positioned/rotated/scaled.
    ctx.global.position_x = 0.5 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.15) * 0.1
    ctx.global.position_y = 0.5 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.11, math.pi / 2.0) * 0.08
    ctx.global.rotation = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.2) * 25.0
    ctx.global.scale = 1.0 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.17) * 0.25
    ctx.global.pivot_x = 0.5 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.09) * 0.2
    ctx.global.pivot_y = 0.5 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.13, math.pi / 3.0) * 0.2
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- bezier: p0/p3 are the endpoints, p1/p2 pull the curve toward them.
    -- Looped here (pingpong) so the arc motion replays continuously.
    --
    -- mt.path.* returns raw (x, y) numbers in whatever coordinate system
    -- the input points used (section 10.7) -- here the points are chosen
    -- directly in offset space (0.5 = no displacement), so the result can
    -- be assigned to offset_x/offset_y as-is. This traces a path relative
    -- to the CHARACTER'S OWN natural position, not a fixed spot on screen:
    -- assigning offset_x/offset_y always moves relative to where that
    -- character would otherwise sit (its geometry.bounds_center), so the
    -- same p0..p3 values trace a different canvas location for a
    -- different character, or if the text/layout changes.
    if ctx.char_count >= 1 then
        local progress = mt.ease.out_cubic(mt.pingpong(ctx.time, 1.5))
        local p0 = { x = 0.5, y = 0.15 }
        local p1 = { x = 0.2, y = 0.55 }
        local p2 = { x = 0.5, y = 0.5 }
        local p3 = { x = 0.5, y = 0.5 }
        local x, y = mt.path.bezier(p0, p1, p2, p3, progress)
        ctx.chars[1].offset_x = x
        ctx.chars[1].offset_y = y
    end

    -- catmull_rom: the curve passes through every listed point exactly, so
    -- 3 waypoints below produce a single continuous path that visits all
    -- 3 of them in order as t sweeps 0 to 1.
    if ctx.char_count >= 2 then
        local waypoints = {
            { x = 0.3, y = 0.75 },
            { x = 0.7, y = 0.4 },
            { x = 0.3, y = 0.3 },
        }
        local progress = mt.cycle(ctx.time, 2.0)
        local x, y = mt.path.catmull_rom(waypoints, progress)
        ctx.chars[2].offset_x = x
        ctx.chars[2].offset_y = y
    end

    -- Fixed CANVAS position instead of character/part-relative offset: to
    -- make a PART travel along ABSOLUTE canvas coordinates (for example,
    -- the same screen path regardless of where its owning character's
    -- glyph naturally sits, or shared waypoints reused across
    -- characters/texts/instances), feed mt.path.* points that are
    -- themselves canvas-normalized (0.5 is canvas center), then pass the
    -- result to mt.layout.place_2d. It resolves the complete 2D hierarchy,
    -- including ctx.global, the owning character, and the part itself.
    if ctx.char_count >= 3 and ctx.part_count >= 1 then
        local character = ctx.chars[3]
        if character.part_count >= 1 then
            -- These parent transforms deliberately animate too. place_2d
            -- compensates for them, so the part still follows the square.
            character.rotation = mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.23) * 35.0
            character.scale = 0.8 + mt.wave(ctx.time, 0.19) * 0.2
            local canvasWaypoints = {
                { x = 0.2, y = 0.2 },
                { x = 0.8, y = 0.2 },
                { x = 0.8, y = 0.8 },
                { x = 0.2, y = 0.8 },
            }
            local progress = mt.cycle(ctx.time, 3.0)
            local canvasX, canvasY = mt.path.catmull_rom(canvasWaypoints, progress)

            local part = ctx.parts[character.part_start]
            mt.layout.place_2d(ctx, part, canvasX, canvasY)
        end
    end
end

Character 2 travels through 3 fixed waypoints along a Catmull-Rom spline that passes exactly through each of them. A part owned by character 3 travels along a fixed square drawn directly in canvas coordinates, using mt.layout.place_2d, while ctx.global itself is being moved/rotated/scaled/pivot-shifted.

name: 22_mt_text.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 4
-- Reference: mt.text.slice -- UTF-8-safe substring extraction. Lua's own
-- string.sub operates on BYTES, so it corrupts any multibyte character
-- (accented Latin, Japanese, emoji, ...) caught mid-sequence. mt.text.slice
-- operates on CHARACTER positions instead, matching ctx.chars indexing.

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    -- 1-based, inclusive character range; endChar defaults to the end of
    -- the string when omitted.
    print("slice(text, 1, 3) =", mt.text.slice(ctx.text, 1, 3))
    print("slice(text, 2) =", mt.text.slice(ctx.text, 2))
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    -- Practical use: highlight the first half of the text differently from
    -- the second half, splitting on a CHARACTER boundary rather than a byte
    -- boundary (safe even if the text contains multibyte characters).
    local halfLength = math.floor(ctx.char_count / 2)

    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        character.fill.use = true
        if index <= halfLength then
            character.fill.color = { r = 1.0, g = 0.6, b = 0.2, a = 1.0 }
        else
            character.fill.color = { r = 0.2, g = 0.6, b = 1.0, a = 1.0 }
        end
    end
end

name: 23_mt_layout_vertical_gap.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 4
-- Reference: verifies the sign of `gap` in vertical mt.layout.reflow.
--
-- The left pair stays at gap = 0. The right pair animates its canvas-height
-- gap from 0 to kMaximumGap and back to 0. Both pairs contain the same glyph,
-- scale, and vertical advance, so the lower-right glyph visibly moves down
-- and back while the left pair remains stationary.
--
-- This script also asserts that relationship every frame. With the old
-- `+ extraGap` implementation in the downward path, the assertion fails
-- because a positive gap makes the pair closer instead of farther apart.

local kControlTargets = { 1, 2 }
local kGapTargets = { 3, 4 }
local kMaximumGap = 0.12
local kGapCycleSeconds = 2.0
local kComparisonTolerance = 0.000001

local function setNaturalCenter(character, targetX, targetY)
    character.offset_x = 0.5 + targetX - character.geometry.bounds_center_x
    character.offset_y = 0.5 + targetY - character.geometry.bounds_center_y
end

local function resolvedOriginY(character)
    return character.geometry.canvas_origin_y + (character.offset_y - 0.5)
end

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    -- Repeating the same glyph makes both pairs geometrically comparable.
    ctx.global.text = "AAAA"
    ctx.global.vertical = true
    ctx.global.tracking = 0.0
    ctx.global.rotation = 0.0
    ctx.global.scale = 1.0
    ctx.global.stretch_x = 1.0
    ctx.global.stretch_y = 1.0
    ctx.global.position_x = 0.5
    ctx.global.position_y = 0.5
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    if ctx.char_count < 4 then
        return
    end

    -- Put the two anchors on the same horizontal guide. The other two
    -- characters are positioned entirely by reflow below.
    setNaturalCenter(ctx.chars[1], 0.35, 0.68)
    setNaturalCenter(ctx.chars[3], 0.65, 0.68)

    mt.layout.reflow(ctx, 0.0, {
        targets = kControlTargets,
        anchor = 1,
        mode = "vertical",
    })
    local gapProgress = mt.smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, mt.pingpong(ctx.time, kGapCycleSeconds))
    local animatedGap = kMaximumGap * gapProgress
    mt.layout.reflow(ctx, animatedGap, {
        targets = kGapTargets,
        anchor = 3,
        mode = "vertical",
    })

    local controlDistance = resolvedOriginY(ctx.chars[1]) - resolvedOriginY(ctx.chars[2])
    local positiveGapDistance = resolvedOriginY(ctx.chars[3]) - resolvedOriginY(ctx.chars[4])
    local measuredGap = positiveGapDistance - controlDistance
    assert(
        math.abs(measuredGap - animatedGap) <= kComparisonTolerance,
        "positive vertical reflow gap must increase downward separation"
    )

    -- Gray is the zero-gap control pair; orange is the positive-gap pair.
    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        character.fill.use = true
        if index <= 2 then
            character.fill.color = { r = 0.65, g = 0.72, b = 0.82, a = 1.0 }
        else
            character.fill.color = {
                r = 1.0,
                g = mt.lerp(0.65, 0.25, gapProgress),
                b = 0.12,
                a = 1.0,
            }
        end
    end
end
description: Reference: verifies the sign of `gap` in vertical mt.layout.reflow.

name: 24_mt_layout_position_branches.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 4
-- Reference: verifies both item branches in mt.layout.place_2d.
--
-- Character objects must use geometry.bounds_center_x/y. Part objects must
-- use geometry.canvas_center_x/y, even though part geometry also exposes
-- bounds_center_x/y. The assertions below verify both formulas every frame.
--
-- Each branch has two identical objects following the same circular target:
-- a large translucent reference placed with the documented formula and a
-- smaller bright object placed by place_2d. Correct calculation
-- keeps the reference visible as an even halo around the bright object for
-- the entire animation. Any position error makes the halo visibly uneven.

local kCharacterCenterX = 0.28
local kCharacterCenterY = 0.68
local kPartCenterX = 0.72
local kPartCenterY = 0.32
local kOrbitRadiusX = 0.1
local kOrbitRadiusY = 0.08
local kAnimationSeconds = 4.0
local kReferenceScale = 1.35
local kComparisonTolerance = 0.000001

local function assertClose(actual, expected, message)
    assert(math.abs(actual - expected) <= kComparisonTolerance, message)
end

local function firstPartOwnedBy(ctx, characterIndex)
    local result = nil
    for index = 1, ctx.part_count do
        local part = ctx.parts[index]
        if result == nil and part.character_index == characterIndex then
            result = part
        end
    end
    return result
end

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    -- Identical glyphs make each reference/test pair directly comparable.
    ctx.global.text = "AAAA"
    ctx.global.vertical = false
    ctx.global.rotation = 0.0
    ctx.global.scale = 1.0
    ctx.global.stretch_x = 1.0
    ctx.global.stretch_y = 1.0
    ctx.global.position_x = 0.5
    ctx.global.position_y = 0.5
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    if ctx.char_count < 4 then
        return
    end

    local animationAngle = ctx.time / kAnimationSeconds * math.pi * 2.0
    local orbitX = math.cos(animationAngle) * kOrbitRadiusX
    local orbitY = math.sin(animationAngle) * kOrbitRadiusY
    local characterTargetX = kCharacterCenterX + orbitX
    local characterTargetY = kCharacterCenterY + orbitY
    local partTargetX = kPartCenterX - orbitX
    local partTargetY = kPartCenterY - orbitY

    -- The first A is the formula-based reference. The second A exercises
    -- the character branch and is rendered on top of the larger reference.
    local referenceCharacter = ctx.chars[1]
    local referenceCharacterGeometry = referenceCharacter.geometry
    referenceCharacter.offset_x =
        0.5 + characterTargetX - referenceCharacterGeometry.bounds_center_x
    referenceCharacter.offset_y =
        0.5 + characterTargetY - referenceCharacterGeometry.bounds_center_y
    referenceCharacter.scale = kReferenceScale
    referenceCharacter.opacity = 0.35
    referenceCharacter.fill.use = true
    referenceCharacter.fill.color = { r = 0.15, g = 0.45, b = 1.0, a = 1.0 }

    local character = ctx.chars[2]
    local characterGeometry = character.geometry
    local expectedCharacterOffsetX = 0.5 + characterTargetX - characterGeometry.bounds_center_x
    local expectedCharacterOffsetY = 0.5 + characterTargetY - characterGeometry.bounds_center_y
    local characterOffsetX, characterOffsetY =
        mt.layout.place_2d(ctx, character, characterTargetX, characterTargetY)

    assertClose(
        characterOffsetX,
        expectedCharacterOffsetX,
        "character branch must use geometry.bounds_center_x"
    )
    assertClose(
        characterOffsetY,
        expectedCharacterOffsetY,
        "character branch must use geometry.bounds_center_y"
    )
    assertClose(
        characterGeometry.bounds_center_x + character.offset_x - 0.5,
        characterTargetX,
        "character branch must reach the animated target x"
    )
    assertClose(
        characterGeometry.bounds_center_y + character.offset_y - 0.5,
        characterTargetY,
        "character branch must reach the animated target y"
    )

    character.fill.use = true
    character.fill.color = { r = 0.2, g = 0.9, b = 0.45, a = 1.0 }

    -- Hide the last two complete glyphs. Only one matching part from each is
    -- shown: the large magenta reference and the smaller yellow test part.
    local referencePart = firstPartOwnedBy(ctx, 3)
    local targetPart = firstPartOwnedBy(ctx, 4)
    for index = 1, ctx.part_count do
        local part = ctx.parts[index]
        if part.character_index >= 3 then
            part.opacity = 0.0
        end
    end

    if referencePart ~= nil and targetPart ~= nil then
        local referencePartGeometry = referencePart.geometry
        referencePart.offset_x = 0.5 + partTargetX - referencePartGeometry.canvas_center_x
        referencePart.offset_y = 0.5 + partTargetY - referencePartGeometry.canvas_center_y
        referencePart.opacity = 0.35
        referencePart.scale = kReferenceScale
        referencePart.fill.use = true
        referencePart.fill.color = { r = 1.0, g = 0.15, b = 0.75, a = 1.0 }

        local partGeometry = targetPart.geometry
        local expectedPartOffsetX = 0.5 + partTargetX - partGeometry.canvas_center_x
        local expectedPartOffsetY = 0.5 + partTargetY - partGeometry.canvas_center_y
        local partOffsetX, partOffsetY =
            mt.layout.place_2d(ctx, targetPart, partTargetX, partTargetY)

        assertClose(
            partOffsetX,
            expectedPartOffsetX,
            "part branch must use geometry.canvas_center_x"
        )
        assertClose(
            partOffsetY,
            expectedPartOffsetY,
            "part branch must use geometry.canvas_center_y"
        )
        assertClose(
            partGeometry.canvas_center_x + targetPart.offset_x - 0.5,
            partTargetX,
            "part branch must reach the animated target x"
        )
        assertClose(
            partGeometry.canvas_center_y + targetPart.offset_y - 0.5,
            partTargetY,
            "part branch must reach the animated target y"
        )

        targetPart.opacity = 1.0
        targetPart.fill.use = true
        targetPart.fill.color = { r = 1.0, g = 0.82, b = 0.1, a = 1.0 }
    end
end
description: Reference: verifies both item branches in mt.layout.place_2d.

name: 25_mt_layout_measure_bounds_2d.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- Reference: mt.layout.measure_bounds_2d for character and part targets.
--
-- The blue "MW" pair rotates and changes scale/stretch continuously. Four
-- orange "+" markers follow the corners of its measured axis-aligned 2D
-- bounds, while the yellow marker follows bounds.center_x/center_y.
--
-- The global transform is also non-identity and animated. If measurement
-- omits global, character, part, pivot, rotation, scale, or stretch, the
-- five markers visibly detach from the transformed target bounds.
--
-- measure_bounds_2d reports transformed natural part boxes before 3D,
-- projection, and Deform. It does not include stroke or shadow extents.

local kCharacterTargets = { 1, 2 }
local kFirstMarkerIndex = 3
local kMarkerCount = 5
local kComparisonTolerance = 0.000001
local kCycleSeconds = 5.0

local function assertClose(actual, expected, message)
    assert(math.abs(actual - expected) <= kComparisonTolerance, message)
end

local function collectOwnedParts(ctx)
    local targets = {}
    for partIndex = 1, ctx.part_count do
        local part = ctx.parts[partIndex]
        if part.character_index == 1 or part.character_index == 2 then
            table.insert(targets, partIndex)
        end
    end
    return targets
end

function OnPreLayout(ctx)
    ctx.global.text = "MW+++++"
    ctx.global.vertical = false

    local angle = ctx.time / kCycleSeconds * math.pi * 2.0
    ctx.global.position_x = 0.5
    ctx.global.position_y = 0.5
    ctx.global.pivot_x = 0.5
    ctx.global.pivot_y = 0.5
    ctx.global.rotation = 8.0 * math.sin(angle)
    ctx.global.scale = 0.9
    ctx.global.stretch_x = 1.05
    ctx.global.stretch_y = 0.95
end

function OnLayout(ctx)
    if ctx.char_count < kFirstMarkerIndex + kMarkerCount - 1 then
        return
    end

    local angle = ctx.time / kCycleSeconds * math.pi * 2.0
    local firstCharacter = ctx.chars[1]
    local secondCharacter = ctx.chars[2]

    firstCharacter.scale = 1.15 + 0.25 * math.sin(angle)
    firstCharacter.stretch_x = 1.2
    firstCharacter.stretch_y = 0.8
    firstCharacter.rotation = 28.0 * math.sin(angle)
    firstCharacter.pivot_x = 0.58
    firstCharacter.pivot_y = 0.43

    secondCharacter.scale = 1.0 + 0.2 * math.cos(angle)
    secondCharacter.stretch_x = 0.75
    secondCharacter.stretch_y = 1.25
    secondCharacter.rotation = -34.0 * math.cos(angle)
    secondCharacter.pivot_x = 0.42
    secondCharacter.pivot_y = 0.57

    mt.layout.place_2d(ctx, firstCharacter, 0.4, 0.52)
    mt.layout.place_2d(ctx, secondCharacter, 0.6, 0.48)

    firstCharacter.fill.use = true
    firstCharacter.fill.color = { r = 0.15, g = 0.55, b = 1.0, a = 1.0 }
    secondCharacter.fill.use = true
    secondCharacter.fill.color = { r = 0.15, g = 0.8, b = 0.95, a = 1.0 }

    -- Omitting targetType selects character indices.
    local characterBounds =
        mt.layout.measure_bounds_2d(ctx, kCharacterTargets)
    assert(characterBounds ~= nil, "character bounds must be measurable")

    -- The explicit "part" form accepts global part indices. Selecting every
    -- part owned by the same two characters must produce the same union.
    local partTargets = collectOwnedParts(ctx)
    local partBounds =
        mt.layout.measure_bounds_2d(ctx, partTargets, "part")
    assert(partBounds ~= nil, "part bounds must be measurable")
    assertClose(partBounds.left, characterBounds.left, "part/character left mismatch")
    assertClose(partBounds.right, characterBounds.right, "part/character right mismatch")
    assertClose(partBounds.bottom, characterBounds.bottom, "part/character bottom mismatch")
    assertClose(partBounds.top, characterBounds.top, "part/character top mismatch")

    local markerPositions = {
        { x = characterBounds.left, y = characterBounds.top },
        { x = characterBounds.right, y = characterBounds.top },
        { x = characterBounds.right, y = characterBounds.bottom },
        { x = characterBounds.left, y = characterBounds.bottom },
        { x = characterBounds.center_x, y = characterBounds.center_y },
    }

    for markerOffset, position in ipairs(markerPositions) do
        local marker = ctx.chars[kFirstMarkerIndex + markerOffset - 1]
        marker.scale = markerOffset == kMarkerCount and 0.32 or 0.24
        marker.fill.use = true
        if markerOffset == kMarkerCount then
            marker.fill.color = { r = 1.0, g = 0.92, b = 0.15, a = 1.0 }
        else
            marker.fill.color = { r = 1.0, g = 0.35, b = 0.08, a = 1.0 }
        end
        mt.layout.place_2d(ctx, marker, position.x, position.y)
    end
end
description: Reference: mt.layout.measure_bounds_2d for character and part targets.

name: 01_fade_up.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- @recommend bg #1e1e1e
-- Showcase: classic lower-third telop. The whole line rises from slightly
-- below its resting position while fading in, holds, then keeps drifting
-- upward as it fades out. A small per-character stagger makes the entrance
-- read left-to-right instead of moving as one rigid block.

local kIntroDuration = 0.7 -- seconds
local kOutroDuration = 0.6 -- seconds
local kFallbackClipLength = 5.0 -- seconds, used when ctx.timeline is unavailable
local kRiseDistance = 0.06 -- canvas-height fraction travelled during the intro
local kExitDistance = 0.05 -- canvas-height fraction travelled during the outro
local kStaggerAmount = 0.35 -- how much of the intro window is spread across characters

function OnLayout(ctx)
    local introAmount, outroAmount =
        mt.timeline.intro_outro_seconds(ctx, kIntroDuration, kOutroDuration, kFallbackClipLength)

    for index = 1, ctx.char_count do
        local character = ctx.chars[index]
        local stagger = mt.distribute(index, math.max(ctx.char_count, 1)) * kStaggerAmount
        local charIntro = mt.ease.out_cubic(mt.saturate(introAmount * (1.0 + stagger) - stagger))
        local charOutro = mt.ease.in_cubic(mt.saturate(outroAmount * (1.0 + stagger) - stagger))

        character.offset_y = 0.5 - (1.0 - charIntro) * kRiseDistance + charOutro * kExitDistance
        character.opacity = charIntro * (1.0 - charOutro)
    end
end
description: Showcase: classic lower-third telop. The whole line rises from slightly below its resting position while fading in, holds, then keeps drifting upward as it fades out. A small per-character stagger makes the entrance read left-to-right instead of moving as one rigid block.

name: 02_typewriter.lua
source:
-- @MugTypography
-- @duration 5
-- @recommend bg #1e1e1e
-- Showcase: typewriter telop. Characters are typed at a fixed real-time
-- rate from the clip start via ctx.output.write_on_*, and near the clip
-- end they are deleted backspace-style at a slightly faster rate. Each
-- newly typed character also pops in with a small overshoot so the typing
-- edge feels mechanical rather than a flat reveal.
--
